question.prompt: Consider systems of three linear equations with unknowns \(x,\) \(y,\) and \(z,\) \[ \begin{cases} a_1 x + b_1 y + c_1 z & = 0 \\ a_2 x + b_2 y + c_2 z & = 0 \\ a_3 x + b_3 y + c_3 z & = 0 \end{cases} \] where each of the coefficients is either \(0\) or \(1\) and the system has a solution other than \(x=y=z=0.\) For example, one such system is \[ \begin{cases} 1 x + 1 y + 0 z & = 0 \\ 0 x + 1 y + 1 z & = 0 \\ 0 x + 0 y + 0 z & = 0 \end{cases} \] with a nonzero solution of \((x,y,z) = (1, -1, 1).\) How many such systems of equations are there? (The equations in a system need not be distinct, and two systems containing the same equations in a different order are considered different.)

solutions.title: Separate repeated and distinct equations
solutions.explanation:
There are only eight possible equations. Systems with at most two distinct equations other than \(0=0\) are easy to handle, leaving a small collection of triples to examine.

The seven equations other than \(0=0\) are
\[
x=0,\quad y=0,\quad z=0,\quad x+y=0,\quad x+z=0,\quad y+z=0,\quad x+y+z=0.
\]
Any system using at most two distinct equations from this list has a nonzero solution. To see why, solve one equation for one variable and substitute into the other. This leaves at most one equation \(Au+Bv=0\) in the remaining two variables. If \(A\) and \(B\) are not both zero, choose \((u,v)=(B,-A)\); if both are zero, choose \((u,v)=(1,0)\). Recovering the third variable gives a nonzero solution. A system consisting only of \(0=0\) also clearly qualifies.

There are \(8^3=512\) ordered systems in total. Exactly
\[
7\cdot6\cdot5=210
\]
have three distinct equations from the seven-equation list. Thus the other \(512-210=302\) systems all qualify.

Now consider three distinct equations from that list, temporarily ignoring their order.

First, suppose none is a single-variable equation. Then the three are chosen from
\[
x+y=0,\quad x+z=0,\quad y+z=0,\quad x+y+z=0.
\]
If all three pair equations occur, adding the first two and subtracting the third gives \(2x=0\), and substitution forces \(y=z=0\). If the total-sum equation and two pair equations occur, subtracting each pair equation from the total-sum equation forces two variables to be zero, and then the third is zero. Therefore no such triple qualifies.

A qualifying triple must consequently contain a single-variable equation. Rename the variables so that this equation is \(x=0\). After substituting \(x=0\), the other six equations fall into three groups:
\[
\{y=0,\ x+y=0\},\qquad
\{z=0,\ x+z=0\},\qquad
\{y+z=0,\ x+y+z=0\}.
\]
The groups impose, respectively, \(y=0\), \(z=0\), and \(y+z=0\). Taking equations from two different groups forces \(y=z=0\). Taking both equations from the same group leaves a nonzero solution.

This produces exactly two types of qualifying unordered triples:

1. Two single-variable equations together with their sum, such as \(x=0,y=0,x+y=0\). There are \(3\) choices for the pair of variables.
2. One single-variable equation, the sum of the other two variables, and the total sum, such as \(x=0,y+z=0,x+y+z=0\). There are \(3\) choices for the single variable.

These types are disjoint, giving \(3+3=6\) unordered triples. Each has \(3\cdot2\cdot1=6\) equation orders, so they contribute \(36\) systems.

The requested total is
\[
302+36=\boxed{338},
\]
choice \(\boxed{\text{B}}\).
